stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary emergency department. A 9 year old girl weighing 30 kg is brought in by her parents with a 3 day history of thirst, polyuria, tummy pain, and vomiting.

She looks unwell but is alert, responds appropriately to questions, and has warm peripheries with capillary refill of 3 seconds. Her mucous membranes are dry and her breathing is deep and slow. There is no recent overseas travel.

Pulse rate 130/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Point-of-care glucose 26 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.15, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-30), blood ketones 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected sodium 143 mmol/L. She has no known diabetes and no prior admissions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130/min; BP 98/62 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; warm peripheries; capillary refill 3 sec; dry mucous membranes; Kussmaul breathing
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 26 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); venous pH 7.15; bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-30); ketones 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6); Na 138 mmol/L (135-145); K 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); corrected Na 143 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 15 minutes, then start deficit rehydration over 24 hours
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is reserved for children with true shock (unresponsive, thready pulses, cold peripheries, hypotension for age); this child is alert with a palpable pulse and warm peripheries, so a smaller cautious bolus is preferred to reduce cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes, then rehydrate over 48 hours with saline and potassium
options.rationale: In a child who is dehydrated but not shocked, the RCH and ISPAD pathway is a 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes followed by controlled rehydration over 48 hours to minimise the fall in serum osmolality and reduce cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022 guidelines).

options.text: Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately and give 0.45% saline maintenance over 24 hours
options.rationale: Insulin is delayed by 1 to 2 hours after fluids commence to avoid a rapid osmolar shift; 0.45% saline is not used until after the initial rehydration phase, and a 24 hour rehydration schedule is faster than the recommended 48 hours (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg intravenously over 30 minutes to correct the acidosis, then commence saline maintenance
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA because it worsens intracellular acidosis, exaggerates hypokalaemia, and is independently associated with cerebral oedema; acidosis resolves with fluids and insulin (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, insert a central line, and start 3% hypertonic saline infusion for cerebral protection
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for children with clinical evidence of cerebral oedema (headache, altered consciousness, bradycardia, hypertension, focal signs), not prophylactically at presentation (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances rehydration against the risk of cerebral oedema, which carries a mortality of 20 to 25 percent. Children who are dehydrated but not shocked receive a modest 10 mL/kg saline bolus and then have their deficit replaced evenly over 48 hours. Insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour starts 1 to 2 hours after fluids commence, and potassium is added once serum potassium is known and urine output is confirmed.
key_points: 10 mL/kg saline bolus for dehydration without shock; 20 mL/kg only for true shock.
Rehydrate over 48 hours to limit osmolar shifts and cerebral oedema risk.
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA, subtract any pre-insulin bolus above 20 mL/kg from the calculated deficit when planning the 48 hour rehydration rate.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the high-dependency unit. A 7 year old girl weighing 24 kg was admitted 5 hours ago with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis. She received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus, was commenced on 48 hour rehydration with 0.9% saline plus 40 mmol/L potassium chloride, and insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour was started at hour 2.

At hour 4 her venous pH had improved from 7.10 to 7.24 and her glucose had fallen from 32 to 14 mmol/L. Over the last 30 minutes the nurse reports she has become drowsy and difficult to rouse and complained of a severe headache before becoming sleepy.

Pulse rate 62/min, blood pressure 140/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C. Repeat glucose is 12 mmol/L, corrected sodium has risen from 141 to 144 mmol/L, and the fluid rate has not been altered. Fundoscopy shows no papilloedema and pupils are equal and reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62/min; BP 140/92 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, difficult to rouse; preceding severe headache; pupils equal and reactive; no papilloedema
data_table.Current therapy: 48 hour rehydration 0.9% saline + KCl 40 mmol/L; insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour started at hour 2
data_table.Trajectory: pH 7.10 to 7.24; glucose 32 to 12 mmol/L; corrected Na 141 to 144 mmol/L over 4 hours

lead_in: What is the single best immediate intervention?

options.text: Give 3% hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg intravenously over 15 minutes and reduce the current fluid rate by one third
options.rationale: The Muir criteria diagnostic combination of altered consciousness, bradycardia for age, hypertension, and preceding headache identifies cerebral oedema; hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes is first-line in Australia when serum sodium has not been falling, and fluid rate is reduced to slow further osmolar shift (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022 guidelines).

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus and add 5% dextrose to the current maintenance and rehydration fluid
options.rationale: A saline bolus increases free water delivery to the brain and worsens cerebral oedema; adding dextrose is appropriate when glucose falls below 14 to 17 mmol/L but does not address the acute neurological deterioration (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion, arrange urgent non-contrast CT brain, and continue current fluids while awaiting imaging
options.rationale: Imaging must never delay treatment of clinically diagnosed cerebral oedema, and stopping insulin risks ketogenesis recurring; the priority is osmotherapy first, imaging after stabilisation (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, place the head of the bed flat, and continue current fluids unchanged
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no role in DKA-related cerebral oedema, which is not vasogenic in the tumour sense; head-down positioning would worsen intracranial pressure (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Intubate for airway protection, hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 25 mmHg, and continue the existing fluid regimen unchanged
options.rationale: Aggressive hyperventilation below a PaCO2 of 30 mmHg is associated with worse neurological outcomes in DKA-related cerebral oedema and does not replace osmotherapy; intubation alone does not treat the oedema (Source: ISPAD 2022 guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clinically apparent cerebral oedema complicates 0.5 to 1 percent of paediatric DKA episodes and carries a 20 to 25 percent mortality with severe neurological sequelae in survivors. The Muir bedside criteria diagnose it before imaging: altered consciousness or headache with bradycardia for age, blood pressure rising rather than falling, or focal neurological signs. Osmotherapy with hypertonic saline (or mannitol) is given immediately, fluid rate is reduced, and imaging follows stabilisation.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis by Muir criteria; do not delay treatment for imaging.
Hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes.
Avoid PaCO2 below 30 mmHg with prolonged hyperventilation.
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia paired with rising blood pressure in a child with DKA is the Cushing response and mandates osmotherapy within minutes, not after imaging.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 12 year old boy weighing 40 kg with new-onset DKA. He received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus, and rehydration fluids have been prescribed. You are about to sign the fluid chart before the insulin infusion is commenced.

He is alert with capillary refill of 2 seconds. He has not passed urine since arrival 45 minutes ago but the bladder is not palpably distended and he has been offered a bottle.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Venous pH 7.10, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-30), glucose 30 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), sodium 134 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline unknown), urea 8.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0). ECG shows sinus tachycardia with normal T wave morphology.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 108/70 mmHg; RR 26/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 2 sec; bladder not palpably distended; has not voided since arrival
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.10; HCO3 6 mmol/L (22-30); glucose 30 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); Na 134 mmol/L (135-145); K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 78 micromol/L; urea 8.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0)
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia; normal T wave morphology

lead_in: Which potassium prescription is most appropriate in the rehydration fluid?

options.text: Add 40 mmol/L potassium chloride to the rehydration fluid before insulin is commenced, regardless of urine output
options.rationale: Adding potassium before urine output is confirmed risks hyperkalaemia in a child with unknown renal function; RCH advises waiting until urine output is documented when the initial potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Withhold potassium from the rehydration fluid until urine output is documented, then add 40 mmol/L potassium chloride
options.rationale: Serum potassium is at the upper limit and urine output is not yet documented; the RCH DKA pathway withholds potassium initially when potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L or before voiding, then adds 40 mmol/L KCl once urine output is confirmed because insulin will drive potassium intracellularly (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Add 20 mmol/L potassium chloride to the rehydration fluid and repeat the serum potassium in 6 hours if stable
options.rationale: The standard replacement concentration in paediatric DKA is 40 mmol/L, not 20 mmol/L, because insulin will drive rapid intracellular potassium shift once commenced, and 6 hours is too long between potassium checks in the first day (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg of 10% and nebulised salbutamol for the presenting hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: There are no ECG changes of hyperkalaemia and the value is only marginally raised; hyperkalaemia treatment in DKA is fluids and insulin themselves, which drive potassium back into cells (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Add 60 mmol/L potassium chloride to the rehydration fluid because total body potassium is depleted in every DKA
options.rationale: Total body potassium is depleted but starting concentrations above 40 mmol/L via a peripheral line risks phlebitis and hyperkalaemia if urine output is inadequate; concentrations above 40 mmol/L require central access and continuous ECG monitoring (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: Children in DKA are always total-body potassium depleted, but presenting serum potassium can be low, normal, or high depending on acidosis and dehydration. Once insulin starts, potassium shifts intracellularly and hypokalaemia can develop rapidly. The RCH pathway withholds potassium if serum potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L or urine output has not been documented, and adds 40 mmol/L KCl to rehydration fluids in all other scenarios.
key_points: Withhold potassium until urine output documented if serum K >5.5 mmol/L.
Standard replacement is 40 mmol/L KCl in rehydration fluid.
Peripheral lines cap potassium at 40 mmol/L; central access required above.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA, hypokalaemia is the commonest metabolic complication of insulin therapy in the first 12 hours; recheck potassium at 2 hours after insulin commences.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 8 year old boy in the emergency department 90 minutes after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure. His mother describes stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for around 90 seconds, with post-event confusion for 10 minutes.

He has since returned to baseline, is playing on the tablet, and complains only of a mild frontal headache. He has no history of head injury, no fever, no rash, and no family history of epilepsy. Development is age-appropriate and school reports are normal.

Vital signs within normal limits and neurological examination is unremarkable including tone, power, reflexes, gait, and fundi. Point-of-care glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8) and a bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with a corrected QT of 400 ms.

data_table.Examination: Fully recovered; normal tone, power, reflexes, gait, fundi
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 400 ms
data_table.Event: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure ~90 sec; post-ictal 10 min; no fever, no head injury

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent non-contrast CT brain in the emergency department before discharge from the emergency department
options.rationale: Urgent CT in a first unprovoked seizure is reserved for focal features, persistent altered consciousness, focal deficit, head injury, or bleeding risk; none of these apply here (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures).

options.text: Start sodium valproate 15 mg/kg per day and arrange outpatient neurology follow-up in 6 weeks for further review
options.rationale: Antiseizure medication is generally not started after a single unprovoked seizure because risk of recurrence in the next 2 years is around 40 percent and treatment does not alter long-term prognosis; valproate is also avoided as first-line in adolescents where possible (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures).

options.text: Discharge with safety advice, arrange outpatient EEG and MRI brain, and refer to paediatric neurology for outpatient review
options.rationale: After a first unprovoked seizure with full recovery, a normal examination, and no red flags, RCH recommends discharge with seizure first-aid advice, outpatient EEG (best within 24 to 72 hours), non-urgent MRI, and neurology review; MRI is preferred over CT because it is more sensitive for structural causes (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures).

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture for cell count, protein, glucose, and herpes simplex virus PCR before disposition
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is indicated for suspected meningitis or encephalitis with fever, altered mental status, meningism, or an infant under 12 months; none of these apply here (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures).

options.text: Admit for 24 hour cardiac monitoring and prolonged video EEG telemetry to characterise the event before discharge
options.rationale: Inpatient video EEG is reserved for children with frequent or diagnostically uncertain events, not a single stereotyped generalised seizure with a normal bedside ECG; outpatient EEG is sufficient (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures).

explanation.summary: A first unprovoked seizure in a child needs a careful history and neurological examination to exclude a provoked cause (electrolyte, glucose, trauma, infection, structural). If the child has fully recovered with a normal examination and no red flags, most guidelines recommend outpatient investigation with EEG and non-urgent MRI, and specialist neurology review. Antiseizure medication is generally deferred because recurrence is around 40 percent and treatment does not change long-term outcome.
key_points: Urgent CT only for focal features, persistent altered consciousness, focal deficit, or trauma.
Outpatient EEG (ideally within 24 to 72 hours) and non-urgent MRI is the standard workup.
Antiseizure medication is not started routinely after a single unprovoked seizure.
explanation.pearls: In first-seizure workup, an EEG within 24 to 72 hours of the event doubles the yield for epileptiform abnormalities compared with delayed studies.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general paediatric clinic. A 6 month old boy is brought in by his parents who filmed several episodes on their phone. They describe brief clusters of movements that started 3 weeks ago and now occur 15 to 30 times per day, mostly after waking.

The video shows him lying on his back and suddenly bringing his arms in and drawing his knees up towards his chest, in clusters of 20 repetitions with a few seconds between each. He cries at the end of each cluster. He was born at term without complications and passed the newborn hearing screen.

On review, he no longer reaches for objects with the enthusiasm he showed 6 weeks ago and no longer laughs at the parents in the way he used to. Vital signs within normal limits. Head circumference is on the 25th centile (previously on the 50th at 2 months). Neurological examination shows mild axial hypotonia. Skin examination shows three hypopigmented macules on the trunk.

data_table.Examination: Axial hypotonia; head circumference 25th centile (down from 50th at 2 months); 3 hypopigmented skin macules on trunk
data_table.Event pattern: Clusters of 20 brief flexor movements; 15 to 30 per day; predominantly on waking
data_table.Development: Loss of social smile and reaching over past 3 to 6 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Same-day neurology referral for admission, urgent EEG within 24 hours, and consideration of vigabatrin therapy
options.rationale: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia is a paediatric neurological emergency because each week of untreated hypsarrhythmia worsens developmental outcome; investigation is inpatient within 24 hours, not routine outpatient (Source: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society

options.text: Reassure the parents that these movements represent benign sleep myoclonus of infancy and review in 3 months
options.rationale: Benign sleep myoclonus occurs only during sleep, resolves on arousal, and does not cause developmental regression; the association with regression and skin findings marks this as an epileptic encephalopathy (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures).

options.text: Prescribe oral omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily for suspected infantile Sandifer syndrome and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Sandifer episodes are dystonic posturing with reflux; they are not clusters of flexor jerks in stereotyped repetitions and do not cause developmental regression (Source: RCH CPG: GORD).

options.text: Arrange outpatient EEG in 6 weeks and metabolic screen through the GP, with review afterwards for planning
options.rationale: The cluster of brief flexor spasms on waking, developmental regression, and hypopigmented macules raises West syndrome from tuberous sclerosis complex; EEG typically shows hypsarrhythmia and vigabatrin is first-line in TSC-associated infantile spasms, with earlier treatment giving better developmental outcomes (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures; Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society

options.text: Commence phenobarbitone 5 mg/kg daily as first-line treatment and arrange outpatient neurology review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is not effective for infantile spasms; first-line options in Australia are vigabatrin (particularly if tuberous sclerosis is suspected) or hormonal therapy such as ACTH or prednisolone, guided by paediatric neurology (Source: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society

explanation.summary: West syndrome is the triad of infantile spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, and developmental regression. It typically presents between 3 and 12 months of age with clusters of brief flexor or extensor spasms, most often on waking. Every week of delay in treatment worsens developmental prognosis, so the workflow is same-day neurology referral, EEG within 24 hours, and first-line vigabatrin (especially with tuberous sclerosis features such as hypopigmented macules) or hormonal therapy.
key_points: Clusters of brief spasms on waking plus developmental regression equals presumed West syndrome.
Vigabatrin is first-line if tuberous sclerosis is suspected; ACTH or prednisolone otherwise.
Every week of delay worsens developmental outcome; EEG within 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: Three or more hypopigmented ash-leaf macules in an infant with new spasms is presumptive tuberous sclerosis and should trigger vigabatrin as first-line while awaiting genetic confirmation.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society

subtopic_detail: Childhood absence epilepsy recognition and treatment
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 7 year old girl has been referred by her school after her teacher reported multiple episodes each hour when she seems to stare and stop what she is doing for a few seconds before continuing.

Her parents had thought she was daydreaming until they noticed it happening several times during a single meal. There is no post-event confusion, no incontinence, and no witnessed limb jerking. Development is age-appropriate and she is in a mainstream class.

In the room, you ask her to hyperventilate for 3 minutes by blowing on a paper windmill. During this, she stops speaking mid-sentence, stares blankly for about 8 seconds with eyelid fluttering, then resumes exactly where she left off with no post-event drowsiness. Neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable and vital signs within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Age-appropriate development; unremarkable neurological examination
data_table.Event characteristics: Multiple daily 8-second staring episodes with eyelid fluttering; no post-event drowsiness; provoked by hyperventilation
data_table.History: No incontinence, no limb jerking, no post-ictal confusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antiseizure medication?

options.text: Ethosuximide, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: The provoked brief staring with eyelid flutter and no post-ictal state is classical childhood absence epilepsy; ethosuximide has the best efficacy-to-side-effect profile in randomised trial data and is first-line when absence seizures occur without generalised tonic-clonic seizures (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures; NICE NG217 epilepsies).

options.text: Carbamazepine, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and phenytoin can worsen absence and other generalised seizures and are contraindicated in idiopathic generalised epilepsies (Source: NICE NG217 epilepsies).

options.text: Sodium valproate, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Valproate is effective in childhood absence epilepsy but is generally avoided as first-line in girls and women of future childbearing potential because of teratogenicity; ethosuximide is preferred in this scenario (Source: NICE NG217 epilepsies).

options.text: Levetiracetam, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is a reasonable second-line option for absence seizures but was inferior to ethosuximide for freedom from failure in the head-to-head paediatric trial and is not first-line for isolated absences (Source: NICE NG217 epilepsies).

options.text: Lamotrigine, titrated slowly to therapeutic dose over 4 to 6 weeks
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has slower titration due to rash risk and lower efficacy than ethosuximide for pure absences in the paediatric trial; it is generally reserved for absence with coexisting generalised tonic-clonic seizures (Source: NICE NG217 epilepsies).

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically presents between ages 4 and 10 with multiple daily brief staring spells, often provoked by hyperventilation, and no post-ictal confusion. EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-wave. Treatment choice is guided by whether generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexist: ethosuximide is first-line for isolated absences, with valproate or lamotrigine used when GTCS also occur.
key_points: Ethosuximide is first-line for isolated absences (best trial evidence).
Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin - they worsen absence seizures.
Provoke absences at the bedside with 3 minutes of hyperventilation.
explanation.pearls: The paediatric childhood absence epilepsy trial found ethosuximide equal to valproate in efficacy but with better attentional side-effect profile.

stem:
You are the GP registrar in a suburban practice. A mother brings her 12 month old son for his routine immunisations. He was born at term and has been well.

He received the standard 2 month, 4 month, and 6 month vaccines uneventfully. Six weeks ago he was admitted to hospital for a febrile illness and received a single unit of packed red cells after an accident in which he lost blood.

He is now afebrile and eating well. Vital signs within normal limits. Examination is unremarkable. His mother has no history of immunosuppression and there is no household contact with immunocompromised individuals. She asks whether he can have his 12 month vaccines today.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; systemically well
data_table.History: Packed red cells 6 weeks ago; on time for prior vaccines; no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunisation plan today?

options.text: Give the meningococcal ACWY and pneumococcal 13v today but defer MMR for a further 4 months
options.rationale: The interval applies only to live viral vaccines; inactivated vaccines like conjugate meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines can be given without delay after blood products (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give all three scheduled vaccines today because 6 weeks is a sufficient washout after packed red cells
options.rationale: The Australian Immunisation Handbook specifies 6 months, not 6 weeks, between blood products and live viral vaccines because immunoglobulin persistence is longer than the acute half-life of transfused red cells (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Defer all three scheduled 12 month vaccines for a further 6 months given the recent packed red cell transfusion
options.rationale: Live viral vaccines such as MMR should be deferred for 6 months after packed red cells because passive antibody in the transfusion can inactivate the vaccine virus; inactivated vaccines are unaffected and can be given on schedule (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give MMR intramuscularly today and hold the meningococcal ACWY and pneumococcal 13v until next month
options.rationale: Not only is the transfusion timing wrong for MMR, but MMR is also administered subcutaneously (or intramuscularly per NCIRS guidance), and there is no reason to defer the inactivated vaccines (Source: NCIRS immunisation).

options.text: Check measles serology today and give MMR only if antibody titre is negative and 6 months have elapsed
options.rationale: Routine serology is not required before scheduled MMR under the NIP; the child is due his primary MMR dose regardless of maternal antibody, and the timing is determined by transfusion interval only (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Recent receipt of blood products can neutralise live viral vaccines through passive antibody, so the Australian Immunisation Handbook mandates set minimum intervals before live vaccine administration. Packed red cells require a 6 month wait before MMR or varicella; intravenous immunoglobulin requires longer intervals (up to 11 months for high-dose IVIG). Inactivated vaccines are unaffected.
key_points: Packed red cells: 6 month wait before MMR or varicella.
Inactivated vaccines (pneumococcal, meningococcal conjugate) can be given without delay.
IVIG requires longer intervals depending on dose (up to 11 months).
explanation.pearls: In an infant recovering from transfusion, give the inactivated vaccines on the due date and diary the MMR for exactly 6 months from the transfusion date to avoid drift.

stem:
You are the ED registrar. A 5 year old immunocompetent boy who attends kindergarten was in close contact with a schoolmate who developed a widespread vesicular rash 2 days ago and was diagnosed with chickenpox. His parents present today, 72 hours after the exposure, asking what should be done.

He is a full-term, previously healthy child. He had a single varicella-containing vaccine dose at 18 months and no boosters since. He is currently well with no fever, no rash, and no respiratory symptoms.

He has no history of eczema and is not on any medication. His younger sister is 6 weeks old, exclusively breastfed, and his mother reports she herself had chickenpox as a child. Vital signs within normal limits and examination unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Well; no rash; no respiratory symptoms
data_table.Vaccination history: Single varicella dose at 18 months; no boosters
data_table.Exposure: Close contact 3 days ago with schoolmate who has chickenpox
data_table.Household: 6 week old sister; mother had chickenpox in childhood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the 5 year old?

options.text: Give a second dose of varicella-containing vaccine today as post-exposure prophylaxis for the schoolmate contact
options.rationale: A single dose is around 80 to 85 percent effective at preventing any varicella and breakthrough infection is possible; a further dose given within 5 days boosts protection and shortens or attenuates any breakthrough illness (Source: NCIRS immunisation).

options.text: Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) intramuscularly today as post-exposure prophylaxis for the school contact
options.rationale: VZIG is reserved for high-risk exposed individuals in whom live vaccine is contraindicated (neonates of susceptible mothers, immunocompromised, pregnant women without immunity); a healthy vaccinated 5 year old does not meet these criteria (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Commence oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 7 days as post-exposure prophylaxis for the school contact
options.rationale: Aciclovir prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in a healthy child after household or school contact; vaccine is preferred within 5 days of exposure (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Reassure the parents that no action is needed today because he had a varicella vaccine at 18 months of age
options.rationale: In an immunocompetent child aged 12 months or older who has had a significant exposure within 5 days, a further dose of varicella-containing vaccine is effective for post-exposure prophylaxis; this child had only one prior dose and completes his schedule usefully in this context (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; NCIRS immunisation).

options.text: Isolate at home for 21 days without vaccination and swab any new vesicular lesions with viral PCR if they appear
options.rationale: Empirical isolation without vaccination misses the 5 day post-exposure window in which vaccine works, and swabbing without lesions has no role in prophylaxis (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: For immunocompetent contacts of chickenpox aged 12 months or older, a dose of varicella-containing vaccine given within 5 days (ideally within 72 hours) of exposure is effective post-exposure prophylaxis and either prevents disease or attenuates severity. VZIG and aciclovir are reserved for those at high risk in whom live vaccine is contraindicated. The Australian NIP schedules varicella at 18 months as part of MMRV; a second dose in later childhood is not routinely funded but is recommended post-exposure or for enhanced protection.
key_points: Post-exposure varicella vaccine within 5 days for immunocompetent contacts aged 12 months plus.
VZIG for neonates of susceptible mothers, immunocompromised, or pregnant women without immunity.
The 18 month NIP MMRV is a single dose; a second dose is not routinely funded.
explanation.pearls: The 5-day post-exposure window for varicella vaccine is counted from first contact, not from rash onset in the source case.

subtopic_detail: Catch-up schedule for the incomplete traveller child
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 4 year old girl who has recently arrived in Australia from overseas with her family. Her interpreter-supported history is that she received BCG at birth and one dose of DTP-HiB-HepB-IPV as an infant.

She is otherwise well, developing appropriately, and attends kindergarten now that she has settled in. There are no documented allergies. Her family plans to travel back to visit relatives in 6 months.

Vital signs within normal limits. Examination is unremarkable. She has no current fever or rash. She has not received any measles-mumps-rubella containing vaccine. The mother has brought a paper immunisation record from her country of origin which corroborates the history.

data_table.Examination: Well; growth and development age-appropriate
data_table.Previous immunisation: BCG at birth; single DTP-HiB-HepB-IPV in infancy; no MMR
data_table.Documentation: Paper record from country of origin corroborates history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her catch-up schedule today?

options.text: Serology for measles, mumps, rubella, hepatitis B, and varicella today, then commence catch-up only if seronegative
options.rationale: Serology is not routinely recommended before catch-up because it delays vaccination, adds cost, and revaccination of an immune child is safe; the Australian Immunisation Handbook advises catch-up based on documented doses (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give only tetanus-diphtheria vaccine today and refer to a public health service for the remainder of the schedule
options.rationale: Comprehensive catch-up is the responsibility of the primary care team and can be administered at the initial consultation using the Handbook calculator; onward referral without any catch-up misses the opportunity (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Restart the entire NIP schedule from birth today, ignoring the paper record from her country of origin
options.rationale: Prior documented doses are counted towards catch-up; restarting from zero would over-vaccinate and delay pre-travel protection (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Delay all catch-up vaccinations until she has been in Australia for 6 months and has established a Medicare number
options.rationale: Refugees and newly arrived migrants qualify for catch-up vaccines free under the NIP regardless of Medicare status; delaying leaves her unprotected for planned travel (Source: NCIRS immunisation).

options.text: Give catch-up vaccines today using the online Handbook calculator, prioritising MMR and DTP-containing vaccines
options.rationale: The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends immediate catch-up using the online calculator, which schedules doses based on age and prior documented doses; MMR and DTP-containing vaccines are the priority in a 4 year old with pre-travel plans (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; NCIRS immunisation).

explanation.summary: The Australian Immunisation Handbook provides a free online catch-up calculator that generates an individualised schedule based on age and documented prior doses. Newly arrived children (refugees, migrants, humanitarian entrants) are eligible for catch-up vaccines under the NIP at no cost regardless of Medicare status. Serology is not routinely required before catch-up: revaccination of already-immune individuals is safe and cost-effective compared with pre-testing.
key_points: Use the online Australian Immunisation Handbook catch-up calculator.
Newly arrived migrants get NIP catch-up vaccines free regardless of Medicare status.
Serology before catch-up is not routine; revaccination is safe.
explanation.pearls: For an under-10 child, MMR minimum interval between doses in catch-up is 4 weeks, faster than the routine 3-month gap used in the primary schedule.

subtopic_detail: Failure to thrive - non-organic red flags
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing an 11 month old boy for his routine review. His mother is worried he is skinny compared with his cousins.

He was born at term weighing 3.4 kg on the 50th centile. Since 4 months of age his weight has drifted down and is now 7.2 kg on the 3rd centile. Length remains on the 25th centile and head circumference is stable on the 50th centile. He was breastfed until 5 months and now takes cow's milk and family food.

He is playful, achieves age-appropriate milestones, and interacts warmly with his mother. Vital signs within normal limits. Examination reveals no dysmorphism, no organomegaly, and no rashes. A food diary shows he grazes on cow's milk from a bottle throughout the day and takes very little solid food. There are no gastrointestinal symptoms and stools are formed and daily.

data_table.Growth: Weight 7.2 kg (3rd centile) from 50th centile at birth; length 25th centile; head circumference 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Playful, warm interaction; no dysmorphism; no organomegaly; no rash
data_table.Feeding: Grazing on bottled cow's milk through the day; minimal solids; formed daily stools

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange dietitian input, structure feeding to three meals and two snacks with cup-only cow's milk, and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Weight faltering with preserved head circumference and length, normal development, and a grazing pattern on cow's milk is the archetypal non-organic feeding-behaviour presentation; dietitian input plus structured mealtimes and cup-only milk is first-line (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth; Growing Strong RCH).

options.text: Order coeliac serology, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, iron studies, and sweat test
options.rationale: Extensive screening at first presentation is low yield when there are no organic red flags; the RCH pathway is a trial of feeding intervention first, then targeted investigation if growth does not respond (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth).

options.text: Admit to hospital for supervised feeding and structured observation to distinguish organic from non-organic causes
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for severe malnutrition, high safeguarding concern, or failure of outpatient intervention; this child does not meet those criteria (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth).

options.text: Prescribe a paediatric high-energy formula supplement 150 mL twice daily to increase daily calorie intake and review growth
options.rationale: Supplement drinks are not first-line and can worsen the grazing pattern by reducing appetite for solids; behavioural feeding modification should be trialled first (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth).

options.text: Notify child protection services today because the growth pattern in this age group is diagnostic of parental neglect
options.rationale: Isolated weight faltering with warm parental interaction and no other safeguarding concerns is not itself grounds for notification; concerns arise if feeding intervention fails, examination shows neglect, or other risk factors coexist (Source: RCH CPG: Child protection).

explanation.summary: Failure to thrive (faltering growth) has organic and non-organic causes; the pattern of growth points to the mechanism. Isolated weight faltering with preserved length and head circumference suggests inadequate energy intake. Excess milk consumption is a common cause because it displaces solid food and iron intake. First-line management is structured mealtimes, cup-only milk (max 500 to 600 mL/day at this age), dietitian input, and close growth review.
key_points: Isolated weight faltering with preserved length and head circumference suggests inadequate calories.
Excess bottled cow's milk grazing is a common cause after 12 months.
First-line is structured feeding with dietitian; empirical investigations are low yield.
explanation.pearls: In toddlers with grazing on cow's milk, cap intake at 500 mL/day to preserve appetite for iron-rich solid foods.

subtopic_detail: Failure to thrive - organic red flags requiring investigation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 22 month old girl is referred by her GP for weight loss and poor growth over the last 4 months.

Her weight has dropped from the 50th centile at 12 months to the 5th centile now, with length falling from the 50th to the 15th centile over the same period. Her head circumference remains on the 50th. Her mother describes intermittent loose stools, a distended tummy after meals, and irritability at mealtimes.

She eats a varied family diet without cow's milk overuse, was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and was previously well. Vital signs within normal limits. Examination shows a distended abdomen without organomegaly, mild wasting of the buttocks, and pale conjunctivae. Her older sibling has type 1 diabetes mellitus.

data_table.Growth: Weight 50th to 5th centile over 4 months; length 50th to 15th; head circumference 50th
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen; no organomegaly; buttock wasting; pale conjunctivae
data_table.History: Loose stools, abdominal distension after meals, irritability; varied diet; no cow's milk excess
data_table.Family history: Older sibling with type 1 diabetes mellitus

lead_in: What is the single most useful initial investigation?

options.text: Full blood count, ferritin, C-reactive protein, and thyroid function tests as an initial screening panel
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis is a differential for failure to thrive with steatorrhoea but is almost always detected on the Australian newborn bloodspot screen; the family history and gastrointestinal pattern point more strongly to coeliac (Source: RCH CPG: Cystic fibrosis).

options.text: Faecal calprotectin and stool microscopy, culture, and sensitivity as first-line for gastrointestinal symptoms
options.rationale: Faecal calprotectin is useful when inflammatory bowel disease is suspected in an older child with bloody stools, weight loss, and raised inflammatory markers; here the pattern more strongly fits malabsorption (Source: RCH CPG: Inflammatory bowel disease).

options.text: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total serum IgA level, on a gluten-containing diet, as first-line
options.rationale: The combination of faltering length and weight, gastrointestinal symptoms, buttock wasting, pallor, and a first-degree relative with type 1 diabetes makes coeliac disease the leading organic cause; anti-tTG IgA with a total IgA is the initial screen because selective IgA deficiency causes false negatives (Source: Coeliac Australia; RCH CPG: Coeliac disease).

options.text: Urine microscopy, culture, and sensitivity plus urea and electrolytes for occult renal or urinary tract cause
options.rationale: Occult urinary tract infection can cause faltering growth in infants, but the gastrointestinal-predominant symptoms and physical signs make this a low-yield first test in a 22 month old (Source: RCH CPG: UTI).

options.text: Empirical trial of a strict gluten-free diet for 6 weeks before any further blood, stool, or urine investigation
options.rationale: Starting a gluten-free diet before testing invalidates serology and biopsy for coeliac disease; children must remain on a gluten-containing diet until diagnostic testing is complete (Source: Coeliac Australia).

explanation.summary: Faltering growth affecting both weight and length, gastrointestinal symptoms, and a first-degree relative with an autoimmune condition raise coeliac disease as the leading organic cause. First-line screening is anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA plus a total IgA level to detect selective IgA deficiency, which causes false negative tTG. Diagnosis is confirmed by duodenal biopsy in most Australian centres, although the ESPGHAN pathway allows biopsy-free diagnosis in selected children with very high titres.
key_points: Screen with anti-tTG IgA plus total IgA to detect selective IgA deficiency.
Do not start a gluten-free diet before testing - it invalidates results.
First-degree relatives with autoimmune disease (T1DM, thyroid) increase risk.
explanation.pearls: A high pre-test probability plus anti-tTG IgA titre above 10 times the upper limit of normal plus positive EMA on a second sample allows biopsy-free coeliac diagnosis under ESPGHAN 2020 criteria.

subtopic_detail: Failure to thrive - short stature discrimination
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5 year old boy in a general clinic. His parents are worried he has been the shortest in his kindergarten class for the last year.

He was born at term with birth weight and length on the 50th centile. From 2 years of age his height has tracked along the 3rd centile, and his weight has tracked along the 10th. Head circumference is on the 50th. His growth velocity over the last year is 6 cm.

He is an active child who eats a varied family diet and has no gastrointestinal symptoms. His father is 165 cm tall (adult height on the 5th male centile) and his mother is 155 cm tall (adult height on the 10th female centile). Vital signs within normal limits. Examination reveals a well-proportioned child with no dysmorphism and normal genital examination.

data_table.Growth: Height 3rd centile (stable); weight 10th centile; head circumference 50th; growth velocity 6 cm/year
data_table.Examination: Well-proportioned; no dysmorphism; normal genital examination
data_table.Parental heights: Father 165 cm (5th centile); mother 155 cm (10th centile)
data_table.History: No gastrointestinal symptoms; varied diet; well child

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for growth hormone stimulation testing and consideration of GH replacement
options.rationale: Growth hormone stimulation testing is reserved for children with subnormal growth velocity, or predicted final height significantly below mid-parental target, or associated features; the growth velocity of 6 cm per year at age 5 is normal (Source: RCH CPG: Short stature).

options.text: Reassure the parents, calculate the mid-parental target height, and review growth in 6 to 12 months without further tests
options.rationale: Growth hormone therapy is PBS-restricted in Australia to specific diagnoses including growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency, SGA without catch-up, and Prader-Willi syndrome; familial short stature is not an indication (Source: PBS growth hormone criteria).

options.text: Order thyroid function, coeliac serology, IGF-1, urea and electrolytes, and a karyotype for chromosomal cause today
options.rationale: Screening panel is indicated when height is significantly below mid-parental target or growth velocity is subnormal; in a child tracking as expected for parental heights, extensive tests are low yield (Source: RCH CPG: Short stature).

options.text: Arrange a bone age radiograph of the non-dominant hand and wrist today to define constitutional delay versus familial cause
options.rationale: Bone age is useful when constitutional delay is suspected (a child whose growth curve suggests catch-up potential); familial short stature has a bone age similar to chronological age and imaging is not required at first presentation with a normal growth velocity (Source: RCH CPG: Short stature).

options.text: Commence recombinant growth hormone empirically to optimise his final adult height and review response in 3 months
options.rationale: A well child tracking parallel to the 3rd centile since age 2 with normal growth velocity, normal proportions, and parents whose adult heights are on lower centiles has familial (genetic) short stature; the mid-parental height calculation contextualises the target and growth review confirms trajectory (Source: RCH CPG: Short stature).

explanation.summary: Short stature is discriminated by growth trajectory, mid-parental height, growth velocity, and body proportions. Familial short stature is characterised by tracking parallel to a low centile from around age 2, with parents whose heights are similarly placed, normal growth velocity, and body proportions. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty shows a delayed bone age and often family history of late puberty. Pathological causes (endocrine, syndromic, chronic disease) usually show a falling percentile or subnormal growth velocity.
key_points: Growth velocity below 4 to 5 cm/year age 4 to puberty warrants investigation.
Familial short stature: tracks parallel to a low centile, normal velocity, short parents.
PBS-restricted growth hormone indications: GHD, Turner, CRI, SGA, PWS.
explanation.pearls: Mid-parental target for a boy = (father height + mother height + 13 cm) / 2; a predicted final height within 8.5 cm of this is consistent with genetic potential.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department. A 5 week old boy is brought in by his parents with a 2 week history of vomiting after every feed.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and is exclusively formula-fed. His mother describes vomits that shoot across the room within minutes of feeding and are non-bilious. Between feeds he seems hungry and takes the next bottle avidly.

He has lost weight from his birth centile: from 3.5 kg at birth to 3.3 kg today. Vital signs within normal limits and he is alert with dry mucous membranes. Serum sodium 135 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 92 mmol/L (95-110), bicarbonate 32 mmol/L (22-30), venous pH 7.48. Point of care glucose is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Alert; dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft
data_table.History: Non-bilious projectile vomits after every feed for 2 weeks; hungry between feeds; formula-fed
data_table.Growth: 3.5 kg at birth to 3.3 kg at 5 weeks
data_table.Investigations: Na 135 mmol/L (135-145); K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); Cl 92 mmol/L (95-110); HCO3 32 mmol/L (22-30); pH 7.48; glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange abdominal ultrasound today and correct fluids and electrolytes intravenously before referring to paediatric surgery
options.rationale: The pattern of non-bilious projectile vomiting in a hungry infant with a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is diagnostic of pyloric stenosis; ultrasound confirms it and electrolytes must be corrected preoperatively because anaesthesia in an alkalotic infant risks post-operative apnoea (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis).

options.text: Reassure the parents this represents physiological posseting and advise thickened feeds with paediatric review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Physiological reflux does not project across the room, does not cause weight loss, and does not produce hypochloraemic alkalosis; delay risks progressive dehydration (Source: RCH CPG: GORD).

options.text: Perform urgent laparotomy for suspected malrotation with midgut volvulus without preoperative imaging or optimisation
options.rationale: Midgut volvulus classically produces bilious vomiting and abdominal tenderness with shock; the non-bilious vomit and alkalosis point away from this diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation).

options.text: Prescribe oral omeprazole 1 mg/kg once daily for suspected severe reflux disease and arrange outpatient review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Anti-reflux therapy does not treat mechanical outlet obstruction; the metabolic picture rules out reflux as the cause and prescribing empirical acid suppression delays definitive care (Source: RCH CPG: GORD).

options.text: Arrange an upper gastrointestinal contrast study and admit for gastric decompression with a wide-bore nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging in Australia because it avoids ionising radiation and is highly accurate; contrast is reserved for equivocal cases or suspected malrotation (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis).

explanation.summary: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically presents at 3 to 6 weeks of age with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds in a hungry baby, weight loss, and a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound is diagnostic (pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm, pyloric channel length >15 mm). Definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after preoperative fluid and electrolyte correction, because operating on an alkalotic infant risks central respiratory depression and postoperative apnoea.
key_points: Classic biochemistry: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Ultrasound is first-line imaging; muscle >3 mm, channel >15 mm.
Correct electrolytes before surgery to prevent post-op apnoea.
explanation.pearls: Target preoperative bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L before pyloromyotomy to minimise post-anaesthetic apnoea risk.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary emergency department. A 9 month old girl is brought in by her parents with a 12 hour history of episodes of screaming and drawing her legs up towards her tummy, occurring every 20 to 30 minutes.

Between episodes she has been sleepy but rousable. She has vomited three times, initially food, then twice with a green colour. Her mother noticed her nappy this morning contained soft brown stool mixed with what looked like red jelly.

Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C. Abdomen is soft between episodes with a palpable long thin lump in the right upper tummy. Capillary refill is 3 seconds. There is no rash. She had rotavirus vaccine on schedule. Point of care glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148/min; BP 92/56 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable between episodes; capillary refill 3 sec; palpable long thin lump in right upper abdomen
data_table.History: Colicky screaming and leg-drawing every 20 to 30 min for 12 hours; three vomits (last two green); nappy with soft brown stool mixed with red jelly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an air-contrast enema in the emergency department before any resuscitation or preliminary imaging is done
options.rationale: Air-contrast enema is performed under radiology guidance after ultrasound confirmation with surgical backup available and after fluid resuscitation, not empirically at the bedside (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Proceed directly to theatre for open manual reduction without preoperative imaging or intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Air-contrast enema is the first-line reduction technique in the stable resuscitated child in Australia; surgery is reserved for failed enema, peritonitis, or perforation (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Give oral ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg, discharge home with reassurance, and arrange outpatient review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting, blood in the stool, and a palpable mass are all surgical red flags; discharge would risk bowel ischaemia and perforation (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline, arrange urgent abdominal ultrasound, and consult paediatric surgery today
options.rationale: The clinical pattern is intussusception; the child is showing early signs of shock so a resuscitation bolus is given, ultrasound provides definitive diagnosis (target sign or pseudokidney), and paediatric surgery is consulted to plan air-contrast enema reduction and surgical backup (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Arrange a nuclear medicine Meckel scan today to identify a lead point for intussusception before any intervention
options.rationale: Meckel scan is used to identify a specific lead point on an elective basis; the priority in an acutely unwell child with intussusception is resuscitation, ultrasound, and enema reduction (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

explanation.summary: Intussusception classically presents between 6 and 24 months with paroxysmal irritability, drawing up of the legs, vomiting (initially non-bilious, later bilious), lethargy between episodes, and blood-mixed stool. Ultrasound is first-line imaging (target or pseudokidney sign). Reduction by air-contrast enema succeeds in around 80 to 90 percent of stable, resuscitated children in tertiary centres, with surgery reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, or perforation.
key_points: Ultrasound first, then air-contrast enema in a resuscitated child.
Bilious vomiting or blood in stool signals late presentation with ischaemia risk.
Surgery for failed enema, peritonitis, or perforation.
explanation.pearls: Recurrence occurs in around 10 percent after successful enema; most recurrences are within 24 to 48 hours, so observation in hospital overnight is standard.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department. A 3 week old girl presents with vomiting after feeds for the last week.

She was born at 37 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy, is exclusively breastfed, and initially fed well. Her mother reports that vomits are effortless, come up soon after feeds, and volumes vary. One vomit yesterday looked green-tinged to the mother but the others have been the colour of milk. She has passed meconium normally and has soft yellow stools.

Her weight has increased from 2.9 kg at birth to 3.4 kg today, tracking along the 25th centile. She is alert, well perfused, and feeds hungrily during your assessment. Vital signs within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows a soft, non-distended abdomen with no palpable masses and no tenderness. No visible peristalsis is seen after a test feed.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, feeds hungrily during review; abdomen soft, non-distended, no mass, no tenderness; no visible peristalsis after test feed
data_table.Growth: 2.9 kg birth to 3.4 kg today (tracking 25th centile)
data_table.History: Effortless vomits after feeds for 1 week; volumes vary; one green-tinged vomit yesterday, otherwise milky; normal soft yellow stools; passed meconium normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with reassurance about physiological reflux and review at the routine 6 week check with the general practitioner
options.rationale: One reported bilious vomit in a young infant is a red flag for malrotation with midgut volvulus that must be excluded before ascribing symptoms to reflux, even when other features look reassuring (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation).

options.text: Arrange an urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to define the position of the duodenojejunal junction today
options.rationale: An upper GI contrast study is the definitive investigation for malrotation because it visualises the position of the duodenojejunal junction (normally to the left of the vertebral pedicle at the level of the pylorus); any history of bilious vomiting in an infant mandates exclusion of malrotation before other diagnoses are entertained (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation).

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound today to measure the pyloric channel length and pyloric muscle wall thickness
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis typically presents at 3 to 6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting, weight loss, and metabolic alkalosis; the reported bilious vomit points away from this diagnosis and towards malrotation (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis).

options.text: Commence a 4 week trial of thickened feeds and omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily for suspected significant reflux disease
options.rationale: Empirical acid suppression is not first-line for physiological reflux and delays exclusion of malrotation; PPIs are reserved for confirmed reflux disease with erosive change or extra-oesophageal complications after specialist review (Source: RCH CPG: GORD).

options.text: Arrange a contrast enema today to exclude Hirschsprung disease as the underlying cause of the reported vomiting
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, and constipation, and typically causes bilious vomiting as part of enterocolitis rather than isolated post-feed vomits with normal stools (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation and Hirschsprung).

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical red flag until proven otherwise, most importantly for malrotation with midgut volvulus, which can progress to bowel infarction within hours. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study visualises the position of the duodenojejunal junction: normally to the left of the vertebral pedicle at the level of the pylorus. If the junction is abnormally positioned or the small bowel loops sit to the right of the vertebral column, a Ladd procedure is required.
key_points: Any bilious vomit in an infant requires exclusion of malrotation.
Upper GI contrast is the definitive study for duodenojejunal junction position.
Progression to midgut volvulus can infarct bowel within hours.
explanation.pearls: In the neonate with even a single reported bilious vomit, the safer path is to accept a low pre-test probability and image, because the consequence of missing volvulus is short-gut syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Developmental delay red flags and referral
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing an 18 month old boy for his routine developmental review. His parents came primarily to ask about ear infections but you use the visit to run through his milestones.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He sits without support but is not yet standing independently, cruises briefly around furniture, and takes one to two steps with hand-holding. He babbles but has no clear words, does not point to show interest, and rarely makes eye contact when called by name.

He was in early daycare 3 mornings a week until 8 months and has been at home with grandparents since then. Vital signs within normal limits. He has bilateral serous middle ear effusions on examination but no acute infection. Hearing was last tested at newborn screen and passed. His weight and height are on the 50th centile and head circumference on the 25th.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral serous middle ear effusions; no acute infection; growth 25th to 50th centile
data_table.Development: Sits unsupported; cruises briefly; 1 to 2 steps with hand-holding; babbles but no clear words; no protodeclarative pointing; poor response to name
data_table.Hearing history: Passed newborn hearing screen; not tested since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe amoxicillin for otitis media with effusion to accelerate resolution and review the child in 2 weeks time
options.rationale: Chromosomal microarray and Fragile X testing are recommended in the workup of unexplained global developmental delay but are ordered after specialist paediatric assessment confirms the developmental phenotype (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay).

options.text: Reassure the parents that boys often talk later than girls and review at the routine 2 year developmental check
options.rationale: Sex-based reassurance is not evidence-based; absent single words, no protodeclarative pointing, and poor response to name at 18 months are M-CHAT-R referral triggers regardless of sex (Source: Australian Autism Alliance).

options.text: Refer to audiology for formal hearing assessment and to community paediatric services for developmental review
options.rationale: The combination of language and social-communication delay in an 18 month old with current serous middle ear effusions requires both a formal audiology assessment (newborn screen does not exclude later conductive loss) and a developmental assessment; both referrals proceed in parallel because either or both may be contributing (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay; Australian Autism Alliance).

options.text: Insert bilateral tympanostomy tubes now because the language delay is driven by the current middle ear effusions
options.rationale: Grommets are considered for persistent bilateral effusions with documented conductive hearing loss over 3 months; they are placed after audiology assessment, and hearing loss does not explain the social-communication features (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Arrange a chromosomal microarray and Fragile X testing today before making any specialist or audiology referral
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not indicated for otitis media with effusion without acute infection; effusions typically resolve spontaneously within 3 months (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

explanation.summary: Language, social-communication, or motor delay identified at a developmental check requires prompt referral for formal hearing assessment and specialist paediatric review. The newborn hearing screen tests for congenital sensorineural loss but does not exclude subsequent conductive loss from otitis media with effusion. Referral pathways in Australia include community paediatric services, Child and Family Health, and NDIS Early Childhood Approach for children under 6.
key_points: Newborn hearing screen does not exclude later conductive hearing loss.
Language, social, and motor delay at 18 months triggers audiology and paediatric referral.
NDIS Early Childhood Approach is the pathway for children under 6 with developmental concerns.
explanation.pearls: Under NDIS Early Childhood Approach, children under 6 with developmental concerns can be referred without a diagnosis and receive early intervention while assessment proceeds.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

stem:
You are the GP registrar in a suburban practice. The practice nurse has completed a M-CHAT-R with the parents of a 20 month old boy at his health check because his mother had raised concern about the way he plays.

He was born at term, is otherwise well, and has met his gross motor milestones. He walked at 13 months. He has a few single words but rarely uses them to request or share, spends long periods lining up his toy cars, becomes distressed if his routine changes, and does not respond to his name most of the time.

Vital signs within normal limits. General examination is unremarkable. His hearing was tested last month by community audiology and was normal bilaterally. The M-CHAT-R score is 8 out of 20, with fails on the critical items for pointing, showing, response to name, pretend play, and joint attention. His mother asks what happens next.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; normal bilateral hearing on recent formal audiology
data_table.Development: Walking at 13 months; a few single words but no requesting or sharing; ritualised play with cars; distress with routine change; poor response to name
data_table.Screening: M-CHAT-R score 8/20; fails on protodeclarative pointing, showing, response to name, pretend play, joint attention

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to community speech pathology alone because the primary problem is expressive language delay in a young boy
options.rationale: Isolated speech pathology referral misses the social-communication cluster and delays access to multidisciplinary autism assessment and NDIS-funded early intervention (Source: Australian Autism Alliance).

options.text: Repeat the M-CHAT-R follow-up interview today to confirm the failed critical items before making any specialist referral
options.rationale: The follow-up interview is used to reduce false positives in the medium-risk band (score 3 to 7); a score of 8 or above already meets the high-risk threshold and referral is not further delayed by re-interview (Source: M-CHAT-R/F).

options.text: Reassure the mother, provide parent reading on encouraging joint attention, and repeat the M-CHAT-R at the 2 year check
options.rationale: A high-risk M-CHAT-R with failed critical items should not be observed for a further 4 months because earlier intervention improves outcomes; concerns raised by parents plus a screen positive at 20 months are actionable now (Source: Australian Autism Alliance).

options.text: Refer for chromosomal microarray, Fragile X, and metabolic screen through the general practitioner before specialist referral
options.rationale: Aetiological workup follows specialist confirmation of the developmental phenotype; ordering genetic tests before assessment adds cost and can delay access to early intervention (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay).

options.text: Refer to a paediatrician or multidisciplinary team for autism assessment and to the NDIS Early Childhood Approach today
options.rationale: A M-CHAT-R score of 8 is in the high-risk band; while a score of 3 to 7 warrants the follow-up interview, a score of 8 or more bypasses the follow-up and mandates direct referral for formal diagnostic assessment and simultaneous early intervention through the NDIS Early Childhood Approach (Source: Australian Autism Alliance; M-CHAT-R/F).

explanation.summary: The M-CHAT-R is a 20-item parent questionnaire validated for autism screening at ages 16 to 30 months. A score of 0 to 2 is low risk; 3 to 7 is medium risk and triggers the follow-up interview to reduce false positives; 8 or more is high risk and warrants immediate diagnostic referral. Early intervention through the NDIS Early Childhood Approach can commence in parallel with diagnostic assessment for children under 6.
key_points: M-CHAT-R scoring: 0-2 low, 3-7 medium (do follow-up), 8-20 high (refer directly).
NDIS Early Childhood Approach accepts referral without formal diagnosis under age 6.
Genetic workup follows specialist confirmation; do not order pre-referral.
explanation.pearls: M-CHAT-R critical items (protodeclarative pointing, showing, response to name, imitation, following gaze) carry more weight; two or more critical fails is high-risk even at a total score below 8.

You are the general paediatric registrar seeing a 2 year old girl for delay across all developmental domains. She was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy.

She sits unsupported but does not yet walk. She has no words and does not point. She can hold a spoon briefly but cannot self-feed. Her mother and father are unrelated and there is no family history of intellectual disability or genetic disorders.

Vital signs within normal limits. She has broad-based gait with a hand-held examiner, and a widely-spaced upper central incisor pattern. Head circumference is on the 3rd centile (was on 10th at 6 months). Formal hearing and vision assessment 2 months ago were both normal. She has been referred to the NDIS Early Childhood Approach.

data_table.Examination: Not walking; head circumference 3rd centile (down from 10th at 6 months); broad-based gait with support; widely-spaced upper incisor pattern
data_table.Development: Delay across gross motor, fine motor, expressive language, social
data_table.Recent tests: Formal hearing and vision normal 2 months ago
data_table.Family history: Unrelated parents; no known intellectual disability or genetic disorders

lead_in: What is the single most useful first-line investigation for aetiology?

options.text: Blood ammonia, lactate, plasma amino acids, and acylcarnitine profile as a metabolic screen for global delay
options.rationale: Metabolic testing has low yield in an otherwise well child with no episodic decompensation, no regression, and a normal newborn bloodspot screen; it is second-tier if microarray and Fragile X are non-diagnostic (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay).

options.text: Standard G-banded karyotype from peripheral blood to detect chromosomal aneuploidy and balanced rearrangements
options.rationale: Karyotype has lower resolution than microarray and misses most microdeletion and microduplication syndromes; it is reserved for suspected chromosomal aneuploidy or balanced rearrangements (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with sedation for structural aetiology in unexplained global delay
options.rationale: MRI is useful but has lower diagnostic yield than microarray for isolated global delay; it is prioritised when there are focal neurological signs, seizures, or microcephaly of unclear cause after first-line genetic testing (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay).

options.text: Chromosomal microarray from peripheral blood to detect copy number variants as first-tier genetic testing
options.rationale: In Australia, chromosomal microarray is the recommended first-tier genetic test for unexplained global developmental delay because it detects copy number variants at higher resolution than karyotype and has a diagnostic yield of around 15 to 20 percent (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay; RACGP guidance).

options.text: Electroencephalogram from a routine 20 minute recording to detect epileptic encephalopathy contributing to delay
options.rationale: EEG is indicated when seizures or an epileptic encephalopathy are suspected; there is no history of seizures here and routine EEG is not part of the initial workup of global delay (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay).

explanation.summary: The Australian first-tier workup for unexplained global developmental delay is chromosomal microarray, with Fragile X testing added particularly in boys or where family history suggests it. Second-tier includes MRI brain, metabolic screen, and consideration of whole exome sequencing through clinical genetics. Formal hearing and vision assessment are always ordered first because sensory deficits masquerade as developmental delay.
key_points: First-tier: chromosomal microarray plus Fragile X in most cases.
Second-tier: MRI brain, metabolic screen, whole exome sequencing.
Always confirm hearing and vision are formally tested.
explanation.pearls: Chromosomal microarray in unexplained global developmental delay has a diagnostic yield of 15 to 20 percent, roughly double that of karyotype alone.
