You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 5 year old boy is referred by his kindergarten teacher for behavioural difficulties in class.

He struggles to sit still, has difficulty following two-step instructions, and becomes explosive when redirected. He has poor peer relationships and does not read social cues. His teacher describes him as clumsy and forgetful of instructions given only minutes earlier.

He has been in the care of his maternal aunt since birth, following removal by child protection. His biological mother has documented heavy alcohol use throughout the first two trimesters of pregnancy and stopped only in the third. Vital signs within normal limits. Head circumference is on the 2nd centile, height on the 25th, and weight on the 25th. Facial examination shows short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, and a thin upper vermilion. Cardiac and abdominal examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference 2nd centile; height 25th centile; weight 25th centile; short palpebral fissures; smooth philtrum; thin upper vermilion; cardiac and abdominal normal
data_table.Behavioural: Hyperactivity, poor 2-step instruction following, explosive when redirected, poor social cognition, clumsy, poor working memory
data_table.History: Documented heavy prenatal alcohol exposure in trimesters 1 and 2; in kinship care since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary FASD assessment clinic using the Australian FASD diagnostic guidelines
options.rationale: Cognitive assessment is important but forms only one arm of the multidisciplinary FASD workup, which also requires facial phenotyping, growth assessment, and structured neurobehavioural evaluation (Source: Australian FASD Diagnostic Guidelines).

options.text: Commence methylphenidate for suspected ADHD today and review the response to stimulant medication in 4 weeks time
options.rationale: Stimulant medication can help attention symptoms in FASD but is prescribed within a specialist multidisciplinary framework because response is variable and adverse effects (irritability, sleep disturbance) can be pronounced; initiating pharmacotherapy without diagnostic clarification is premature (Source: Australian FASD Diagnostic Guidelines).

options.text: Reassure the aunt that the behaviour will settle with additional structure at kindergarten and review in 6 months
options.rationale: The physical features and developmental profile are unlikely to resolve with school-based intervention alone; early identification of FASD gives access to funded supports and improves adaptive outcomes (Source: Australian FASD Diagnostic Guidelines).

options.text: Refer to a clinical geneticist for chromosomal microarray and Fragile X testing as the priority aetiological workup
options.rationale: Genetic testing is worthwhile as part of a broader workup but is not the priority when a confirmed teratogenic exposure explains the phenotype; FASD diagnosis proceeds first, with genetic testing as a rule-out step (Source: Australian FASD Diagnostic Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange a formal cognitive assessment through the local school psychology service alone as the initial approach
options.rationale: The combination of confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure, three sentinel facial features, growth impairment (head circumference), and neurobehavioural impairment across multiple domains meets the Australian FASD diagnostic pathway threshold and warrants multidisciplinary confirmation and management planning (Source: Australian FASD Diagnostic Guidelines; NHMRC alcohol guidelines).

explanation.summary: The Australian FASD Diagnostic Guidelines require severe impairment in at least three of ten defined neurodevelopmental domains, and split diagnoses into FASD with three sentinel facial features and FASD with fewer than three sentinel facial features. Confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure supports the diagnosis but is not required if all three sentinel facial features are present. Assessment is multidisciplinary and access to funded supports (NDIS, education, mental health) improves long-term outcomes.
key_points: Three sentinel facial features: short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion.
Diagnosis requires severe impairment in 3+ of 10 neurodevelopmental domains.
Multidisciplinary assessment; do not commence stimulants pre-diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: The NHMRC 2020 alcohol guidelines advise no alcohol in pregnancy or while planning pregnancy - there is no safe threshold for foetal alcohol exposure.

You are the GP registrar in a suburban Sydney practice. A pregnant 26 year old woman at 32 weeks gestation attends for an antenatal review with her regular obstetric appointments deferred.

She reports drinking around six standard drinks per day since before she knew she was pregnant, and continuing until 2 weeks ago when she was told about foetal alcohol effects. She now attends today wanting to stop but reports morning tremor and anxiety when she does not drink. She lives with a partner who also drinks heavily. There are no other children at home.

She is medically well, engaged in the consultation, and asks for help. Vital signs within normal limits. Examination reveals no jaundice or abdominal tenderness. She is not intoxicated at the time of consultation. She has not previously been engaged with drug and alcohol services and has never been reported to child protection services.

data_table.Examination: Engaged, not intoxicated; no jaundice; no abdominal tenderness
data_table.History: 32 weeks pregnant; six standard drinks/day continued into pregnancy; last drink 2 weeks ago; morning tremor and anxiety on abstinence; partner drinks heavily; no other children; not previously known to D&A services or child protection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action regarding reporting today?

options.text: Submit a Report of Concern only after the baby is born and any physical features of FASD are documented postnatally
options.rationale: Prenatal reports are specifically permitted in NSW to allow multidisciplinary planning before birth; waiting until postnatal features are visible loses the opportunity to arrange antenatal support (Source: NSW MRG - Mandatory Reporter Guide).

options.text: Submit a prenatal Report of Concern to the Department of Communities and Justice and refer to perinatal drug and alcohol
options.rationale: In NSW, a prenatal Report of Concern to the Department of Communities and Justice is appropriate when there is a reasonable suspicion the unborn child will be at risk of significant harm after birth (here, ongoing heavy alcohol dependence with withdrawal features and a heavy-drinking partner); it triggers early planning without removing legal protections, and perinatal drug and alcohol referral addresses the immediate withdrawal risk (Source: NSW MRG - Mandatory Reporter Guide; NSW Health Perinatal and Family Drug Health Services).
source_refs: NSW Health Perinatal and Family Drug Health Services

options.text: Manage privately with brief motivational counselling and defer any reporting because she has engaged with today voluntarily
options.rationale: Voluntary engagement does not remove the mandatory reporting threshold when risk of significant harm is present; brief counselling alone underestimates the biomedical severity of alcohol dependence with withdrawal at 32 weeks (Source: NSW MRG - Mandatory Reporter Guide).

options.text: Prescribe outpatient diazepam-based home detoxification and review in 1 week without any specialist or child protection referral
options.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal in the third trimester carries risks of foetal distress and preterm labour and is generally managed in an inpatient setting with obstetric input; outpatient benzodiazepine detoxification in this scenario is not safe as first-line (Source: NSW Health Perinatal and Family Drug Health Services).
source_refs: NSW Health Perinatal and Family Drug Health Services

options.text: Contact NSW Police to have her admitted involuntarily today for the safety of the pregnancy and the unborn child
options.rationale: Police involvement is not the appropriate pathway; a woman requesting help can be engaged voluntarily through perinatal drug and alcohol services with a parallel prenatal Report of Concern (Source: NSW MRG - Mandatory Reporter Guide).

explanation.summary: In NSW, the Mandatory Reporter Guide operationalises the threshold of "risk of significant harm" for reports to the Department of Communities and Justice. Prenatal reports are permitted and encouraged when there is reasonable suspicion of postnatal harm, enabling multidisciplinary antenatal planning. Alcohol dependence in pregnancy with withdrawal features is a Perinatal and Family Drug Health Services referral, typically inpatient in the third trimester for foetal safety.
key_points: Prenatal Reports of Concern are supported in NSW for high-risk unborn children.
Voluntary engagement does not remove the reporting obligation when risk is present.
Third-trimester alcohol withdrawal is typically inpatient with obstetric input.
explanation.pearls: Using the online NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide decision tree is best practice; it documents the reasoning and produces the recommended action (report, monitor, refer).
